evidence.text: The Han-dynasty Shuowen entry reads “地之數也。从偶一。凡二之屬皆从二” (“the number associated with earth; formed from paired ones”). Duan Yucai’s Qing commentary corrects 偶 to 耦 and explains 耦一 as doubling the stroke 一. This is a historical account of two equal strokes, not independent proof of how the graph first arose.

evidence.text: The page catalogs forms under Shang, Western Zhou, Spring and Autumn, Warring States, Chu/Qin slips, Shuowen small seal, and clerical script, and describes the graph as two parallel strokes representing two. It attributes the collected forms mainly to Richard Sears’s Chinese Etymology site, which in turn draws on oracle-bone, bronze, Shuowen and other collections. The page does not itself give dated individual 二 inscriptions or establish a detailed sequence of graphic changes; no glyph image was visually inspected in this research.
evidence.title: 二 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.text: The dictionary characterizes 二 in ancient writing as two horizontal strokes used as a primitive counting sign, and lists oracle-bone, bronze, Chu slip/silk, Shuowen, Qin slip, clerical and regular-script form categories. This supports a straightforward numeral-sign analysis; its simplified listing is not a dated inscriptional history.

evidence.source: 漢典 (zdic.net), 二 entry quoting early texts
evidence.text: The dictionary quotes the *Analects* (“聞一以知二,” hear one and know two), *Han Feizi*, and *Yijing* commentary for the numeral value; these references show early textual use but are not themselves dated manuscript witnesses. It separately cites Du Fu’s Tang poem 石壕吏 for 二 meaning ‘second’ in 二男, and the *Zuo zhuan* for 二心, ‘divided/disloyal heart.’ The extensions to ordinal ‘second’ and ‘double-minded’ are attested as usages, but their precise paths and earliest dates are not demonstrated there.

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 二, Middle Chinese and Old Chinese comparison tables
evidence.text: Standard Mandarin is listed as èr (Hanyu Pinyin); Standard Cantonese as ji6 (Jyutping). The page gives Middle Chinese Baxter transcription nyijH and Guangyun category 日母、脂韻、去聲、開口三等, with fanqie 而至切. It compares Zhengzhang Shangfang’s Middle Chinese /ȵiɪᴴ/ and Old Chinese *njis (2003 system) with Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *ni[j]-s (2014 system). These are reconstructions in distinct systems, not a single interchangeable form.

Its readings corroborate the modern and medieval character readings; it makes no claim about a separate object name or a phonetic-component borrowing.

evidence.text: The entry reports a Proto-Sino-Tibetan proposal *kV-ni-s and comparisons with Tibetan, Sikkimese, Tangut, Burmese and Nuosu forms, and notes a newer proposal involving a stop coda based on Bai cognates and Han-era transcriptions. These are lexical reconstruction claims about the spoken numeral, not graphic explanations. The entry gives no primary comparative source inspected here sufficient to assess the proposed cognacy or coda in detail.

gaps: No individual oracle-bone or bronze inscription image for 二 was inspected, and no dated inscriptional witness was verified. Although secondary character-form lists include Shang and later categories, the earliest attested occurrence and exact graphic sequence remain unestablished here.

The Shuowen’s ‘earth’s number’ cosmological framing is an ancient explanation; it does not establish that the graph originally depicted earth. The simpler numeral-stroke account is compatible with the graphic form, but no primary paleographic argument was inspected to adjudicate historical formation.

The cited earliest textual examples are quotations attributed to classical works, not independently dated surviving manuscripts. Exact chronology for the numeric sense and the ‘second’ and figurative ‘double-minded’ extensions remains open.

No proposed phonetic component occurs in this character: 二 is a standalone numeral graph. Therefore no component-by-component sound role or origin_relation applies. Whole-character lexical comparative proposals remain distinct from graphic formation.
The Proto-Sino-Tibetan cognate set and newer coda proposal were found in a secondary entry; the underlying comparative sources and competing analyses were not examined.
